Table 1 reports voice-versus-text coefficients (clustered SEs): message count, Model 3, 1.490*** (0.090); word count, Model 4, 263.4*** (12.700); unique word count, Model 5, 48.2*** (3.180); type-token ratio, Model 6, -0.114*** (0.004); raw lexical diversity, Model 7, 0.262*** (0.023); word-count-adjusted lexical diversity, Model 8, -0.042* (0.018). confirmed: The source read is the local full-text preprint PDF, with 16 pages and Supporting Information on pp. 10-16, including the representative transcripts. The title and authors match the form; no manuscript date or arXiv version number is printed. The source.version wording is supported (PDF p. 1, title and author block; pp. 10-16, Supporting Information).

S1 modality selection was not randomized: students chose voice or text for each interaction, and the authors explicitly limit the findings to associations. The observational context classification is correct (PDF p. 3, Approach; p. 10, Modality Switching Across Successive CAiSEY Sessions).

There is a randomized human study embedded in the same course dataset: after a student chose voice, the perceived gender of the AI voice was randomly assigned female or male, and the authors report results for output outcomes. This is an AI-configuration comparison in ordinary coursework, supporting field_rct and referral to the two-screener pipeline; S1 and S2 are not independent samples (PDF pp. 2-3, Approach; p. 5, Findings; p. 10, Descriptive Statistics).

The final analytic sample contains 203 MBA and EMBA students, 957 conversations, and 16 case-based assignments. There are 458 voice conversations and 499 text conversations; within voice, 240 conversations have a female AI voice and 218 have a male AI voice. The form correctly distinguishes conversation counts from people and does not label 203 as randomized (PDF p. 10, Sample Preprocessing and Descriptive Statistics).

The paper states that 186 of 203 students, or 92%, used both modalities. This documents more than 50 voice users, so the embedded comparison is not identified as a fewer-than-50-person experiment. Exact unique-person counts by modality and voice gender, the number of people at randomization, and a separate sample size for each voice-gender outcome analysis are not supplied; do not replace these with conversation counts (PDF p. 3, Approach; p. 10, Descriptive Statistics; p. 5, narrative voice-gender result).

S1-O1 reported values match Table 1: Model 10, word-count-adjusted semantic diversity, 0.178*** with clustered SE 0.032; Model 9, raw semantic diversity, 1.4*** with clustered SE 0.058. The table defines *** as p<0.001. These are OLS coefficients with user and case fixed effects and standard errors clustered by user and case, not standardized effect sizes (PDF p. 9, Table 1, Models 9-10 and notes; p. 6, Materials and Methods).

S1-O2 reported values match Table 1: Model 2 semantic dissimilarity, 0.005 with clustered SE 0.009; Model 1 lexical dissimilarity, -0.007 with clustered SE 0.005. The Findings report no significant modality difference, and exact contrast p-values are not printed (PDF p. 9, Table 1, Models 1-2; p. 4, Findings).

All text measures use concatenated user messages. Originality compares the conversation with its case reading. Semantic diversity uses similarities among embedded chunks within that conversation, with the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 SentenceTransformer model; it does not compare different participants. Coding the ideational-breadth outcome as flexibility/with_ai and originality as novelty/with_ai is supported (PDF pp. 11-12, Text Extraction, Content Originality, and Divergent Ideation).

S2-O1 accurately summarizes the narrative finding of no evidence that randomized AI voice gender affects any outcome. The PDF supplies no separate voice-gender numerical results table, coefficient, standard error, exact p-value, or arm means; this is not evidence that the effect is exactly zero (PDF p. 5, Findings, final paragraph; pp. 8-12, Figure 1, Table 1, and Supporting Information).

The one_line_finding is supported: 203 analyzed students and 957 self-selected debates; the positive adjusted voice-versus-text association is 0.178, clustered SE 0.032, p<0.001; the randomized voice-gender finding is narrative only. The wording correctly describes the modality result as an association (PDF p. 10, Descriptive Statistics; p. 9, Table 1, Model 10; p. 5, Findings).

This is an original empirical study, not a synthesis; the synthesis defaults do not omit a study count or pooled estimate. The underlying generative model and a downloadable data/code URL are not stated in the document (PDF pp. 2-3, Approach; p. 6, Materials and Methods; pp. 10-16, Supporting Information).
summary: The embedded randomized voice-gender comparison qualifies for the two-screener pipeline, while voice versus text is observational. The reported numbers and source description are accurate, but the design label, exclusions, conversation-count fields, primary-outcome designation, and outcome coverage need correction.
